rationale: A wins because it keeps finding real conflicts inside the supplied facts instead of decorating them. Its line, "The sensors are in the cover. Knowing your blood oxygen costs the top subscription tier," is a clean consumer-tech story with proof holes named honestly. B has usable bones, but "Your mattress now watches your blood oxygen. Doctors have questions" is padded with unsupplied apnea prevalence, wrist-device controversy, and fake price precision.
gaps_in_A: "Eight Sleep's bed now tracks the same signals doctors use to screen for sleep apnea" leans on a medical framing not explicitly supplied; it is likely useful, but it needs backup before becoming the spine of a health pitch.
"the protagonist is the existing owner being asked to pay again" assumes an existing-owner conflict before confirming whether current covers already have the sensors or require new hardware.
gaps_in_B: "sleep apnea, which affects tens of millions of adults, most undiagnosed" imports a prevalence claim not supplied in the update.
"On a $3,000 mattress" invents fake precision from the provided fact that the product costs several thousand dollars.
"consumer health companies routinely commission studies designed to validate features rather than test them" is a sweeping accusation with no support in the given facts.
"the exact fact pattern that draws FDA warning letters" overstates regulatory risk from the update; wellness-not-diagnostic is a tension, not proof of an FDA-warning pattern.
